name: Marco Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Costa's Field with my dad, who's semi-retired and still thinks he's in charge. It's 45 hectares: about 120 outdoor pigs, field vegetables, and a veg box scheme that goes out to 300 households on Thursdays. My mornings are pigs and planning, afternoons are picking and packing. I run the whole box scheme off an AI assistant now, the orders, the route, the emails when the courgettes fail. My partner Ana is a part-time nurse, and our boys, Leo and Tomas, are ten and seven.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mud and margins. The pigs churn the field to soup every winter and the supermarket price for pork hasn't moved in years. The box scheme is what keeps us afloat. I'm also trialling a little solar weeding robot from the growers' co-op, which I adore and my dad calls the Roomba.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. I'd be a bit gutted, honestly. I was counting on the robots to take the worst of the mud off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Online I'd say shame, the tools were just getting good. At the growers' co-op I'd tell people to keep using what works, because the AI that runs my box scheme orders already saves me a day a week. I'd still push the co-op to buy more weeding robots if they pay their way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changing isn't great for us either. Pork's the same price it was six years ago and feed isn't, so the pigs barely pay for themselves. The veg box scheme keeps us afloat, and I was hoping to grow it to 500 households before Dad finally stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the AI doing demand forecasts for the boxes, so we stop composting courgettes. I'd keep the weeding robot on trial and send the co-op feedback every month. I'd try to sign up another 80 households by spring with a cheaper half-box, and keep saving 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not frightened, just stuck with the same thin margins and a lot of mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when your dad does stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day my dad stops, I lose about thirty free hours a week, because Dad doesn't take a wage. Paying someone for those hours would cost maybe 12,000 a year we don't have. That's the number I actually lie awake on, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about the pigs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would say drop the pigs and do veg only, and some nights she's right. Then a family orders three kilos of our sausages for a christening and I remember why we keep them.

say: Shame, the tools were just getting good, and the AI on my box scheme saves **a day a week**.
Keep using what works, and keep buying **weeding robots** if they pay their way.
think: Pork prices haven't moved in **six years** while feed has, so the pigs barely pay for themselves.
The **veg box scheme** is what keeps us afloat.
The real worry is the day **my dad stops** working for free.
do: Sets the AI to **forecast box demand** so fewer courgettes get composted.
Keeps trialling the co-op's **weeding robot** with monthly feedback.
Aims for **80 more households** with a cheaper half-box, and keeps saving 150 a month.
feel: **A bit flat** and stuck rather than frightened, with the same thin margins and mud.
S0.quote: The day my dad stops, I lose about thirty free hours a week, because Dad doesn't take a wage.
fieldNote: Marco would be **disappointed** by AI stalling, because he was counting on robots for the hard labour.
His real worry is his father's **unpaid hours**, which would cost about 12,000 a year to replace.
The pigs barely pay, and he keeps them **partly out of pride**.

steps.text: Set the AI to forecast veg box demand and cut waste
Keep trialling the co-op's solar weeding robot and report monthly
Keep saving 150 a month towards covering Dad's hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's more like it. The thinking tasks are where I already use AI, so I'm ahead there. Robots being slower just means my back hurts for a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the growers' forum I'd say this is the moment for small farms to share the tools, because the admin cost of a box scheme just fell to almost nothing. I'd also say the office jobs in town are the ones feeling it now. We're fine, they're not, and they're our customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI taking over orders, emails and customer questions is basically my box scheme handed to me on a plate. What I watch is the town, because half our 300 households work at the council, the bank or the insurance office. A veg box at 22 a week is the first treat people drop when the office jobs in town cut hours. I'd guess we'd lose thirty or forty boxes, not the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand all the box admin and customer emails to the AI in the first month and use the time on a Saturday market stall to find new customers. I'd put about 3,000 into a co-op share of two weeding robots when they come, keeping two months of money back. And I'd hold off the jump to 500 boxes until I see what the town does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit uneasy. I like the tools, and I don't like guessing which of my customers is about to get a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which customers would you think of first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Okonjo family on Mill Lane, both of them at the insurance office, three kids, the big box every week. When they paused for a month last year it was because one of them was off sick. I'd notice their order before I'd notice the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're fine and they're not. Is that really true for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. Ana's nursing isn't going anywhere, and the AI makes my week shorter. If forty boxes go and the pork price stays dead, it's a tight year, not a lost farm.

say: This is the moment for small farms to **share the tools**, because box scheme admin now costs almost nothing.
The **office jobs in town** are feeling it now, and those people are our customers.
think: AI taking over orders, emails and questions hands me my box scheme **on a plate**.
If the council, bank and insurance office cut hours, I'd guess we lose **thirty or forty** of 300 boxes.
do: Hands all **box admin** and customer emails to the AI in the first month.

Holds off **growing to 500 boxes** until he sees what the town does.
feel: Uneasy about **which customers** are about to lose hours.

fieldNote: Marco reads the new card as **good news** for his own work, since it names exactly the box scheme's admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office jobs go first and the muddy ones last. Huh. That flips it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers aren't the first in line this time, the desk jobs are, and we should be making noise for the people who lose them in 2028. At the growers' co-op I'd say we've got about three years before the robots, so this is the moment to buy shared kit before the big farms get it. Online I'd keep banging on about an AI dividend, a payment to everyone from the money the machines make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own work is mostly hands-on, so I've got till 2031 before a robot can pick a courgette as well as me. The box scheme admin I already hand to the AI, so 2028 makes that bit even easier. What scares me is my 300 households. Half my veg box customers work in offices in town, and if they lose their pay in 2028, the first thing they cancel is a 22-a-week veg box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd do is stop the plan to grow to 500 boxes and hold onto our cash instead. I'd add a cheaper 'basics' box at about 12 a week, so people who lose work can drop down instead of quitting. I'd still put about 3,000 into the co-op's shared weeding robots, half what I'd planned, and keep two months of money back. I'd start a Saturday market stall in town, so I'm not relying on one kind of customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but wide awake. It's the feeling of a storm coming when you've still got time to get the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your box list are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman on the Thursday round who does claims at an insurance firm, she's ordered every week for six years and leaves a note when the eggs are good. That's exactly the kind of job the AI takes in 2028. I'd rather give her a box on credit than lose her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got three years before your own work is touched. Doesn't that feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, yes, about my own hands. But a farmer with steady hands and no customers is just a man with a nice garden. The three years are for getting the customers through, not me.

say: Farmers aren't first in line this time; **the desk jobs** are, and we should speak up for them.
Small farms have about **three years** to buy shared kit before the big farms get robots.
think: My own work is mostly hands-on, so I've got **until 2031**, and the box admin only gets easier.
Half my **300 households** work in offices, and a 22-a-week veg box is the first thing they'd cancel.
do: Halts the plan to grow to **500 boxes** and adds a cheaper basics box at about 12 a week.
Puts about **3,000** into the co-op's shared weeding robots, keeping two months of money back.
feel: **Anxious but wide awake**, like a storm coming while there's still time to get the hay in.
S2.quote: Half my veg box customers work in offices in town, and if they lose their pay in 2028, the first thing they cancel is a 22-a-week veg box.
fieldNote: Marco saw quickly that thinking AI hits **his customers' office jobs** three years before robots touch his own.
His plans are all about **keeping his buyers**, not protecting his own labour.
He still invests in robots, just **more carefully** than in the steady scenario.

steps.text: Drop the 500-box growth plan and add a 12-a-week basics box
Start a Saturday market stall in town for a second set of customers
Put about 3,000 into the co-op's shared weeding robots, keeping two months back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and then three more. That's enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version small farms can win, if we buy the machines together and early. I'd tell the co-op we need a plan for 2034 written by next spring. And I'd push for cheap public loans for shared robots, so we own them instead of renting them from a big company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. By 2031 the AI does all the planning, by 2034 the robots do the digging, and I'd be 51 and running a farm that people visit as much as buy from. My worry is still the customers, but five years gives the town time to find its feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd put about 4,000 into shared robots through the co-op and keep two months of savings. I'd let the AI plan the crop rotations and the box routes completely. With Ana I'd start planning school visits and a pick-your-own patch for 2028, so there's a part of the farm that's about people, not just veg.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Uneasy only when I think about the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad make of school visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble and then be the star of it. My dad's got sixty years of stories about pigs escaping onto the main road, and kids would love him. A robot can weed a bed, but it can't make a ten-year-old laugh about a runaway sow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said uneasy about the town. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the basics box going and give the co-op's surplus to the food bank instead of composting it. It's small. But if we're the ones doing well out of robots, we'd better share some of it.

We need **cheap public loans** for shared robots, so we own them instead of renting them.
think: This is **good for me**: the AI plans by 2031 and the robots dig by 2034.
I'd run **a farm people visit** as much as buy from, and the town gets time to find its feet.

Hands **crop rotations** and box routes fully to the AI.
Plans **school visits** and a pick-your-own patch with Ana for 2028.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, uneasy only when he thinks about the town.
S3.quote: A robot can weed a bed, but it can't make a ten-year-old laugh about a runaway sow.
fieldNote: With eight years before robots, Marco sees **opportunity** rather than threat.
His plan turns the farm toward **visitors**, with his father's stories as part of the offer.
He feels doing well out of robots brings **a duty to share**.

steps.text: Put about 4,000 into shared co-op robots, keeping two months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years to robots. Leo would be 23.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. At the co-op I'd say let's teach this ourselves rather than wait for the dealers. I'd keep pushing the AI dividend idea, because the end point is the same even if it comes slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd love this. I'd use the AI to plan everything from day one and have shared robots on the farm well before 2039. The only thing I'd miss is coming in filthy, if robots do all the dirty work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short agricultural robotics course at the college, about 600, in the first year so I could teach other growers later. I'd save 50 a month for each of the boys' training. I'd add a robot pig feeder through the co-op by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and pretty excited. Like a long run-up to something I've wanted for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd miss coming in filthy. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's how I know I've worked. I like coming in filthy, and Ana makes me strip off in the porch. If robots do the dirty work, I'll have to find something else to be proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Leo and Tomas to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever they love, honestly, but I'd want them to understand machines. Leo already takes apart the weeder when I'm not looking. If my son ends up fixing robots for the whole valley, I'd be thrilled.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, and we'd be idiots to waste it.
The co-op should **teach this ourselves**, and an AI dividend still matters because the end point is the same.
think: I'd love this, with **AI planning everything** from day one and shared robots well before 2039.
The only thing I'd miss is **coming in filthy** once robots do the dirty work.

fieldNote: With the long timeline Marco is **purely positive** about his own future.

He wants to **teach the new machines**, and his eldest son shows the same curiosity.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of the robots, but because my customers in the offices would lose their jobs three years before a robot could even pick a courgette, and before anyone sorted out how to share the money. What would help is a proper AI dividend paid to everyone, and cheap co-op loans so small farms can own their machines instead of renting them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who's going to buy the food. Everyone asks if farmers survive. But a farm with no customers is just a garden.

headlineQuote: A farm with no customers is just a garden.
portrait: Marco Costa, 43, runs **Costa's Field**, a pig and vegetable farm with a 300-household veg box scheme, with his unpaid father.
He **uses AI every day** and is trialling a weeding robot.
If AI stalls he's **uneasy**, stuck with flat pork prices and dreading the day his father stops.
Under steady change he's **mostly excited**, uneasy only about office-worker customers dropping their boxes.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious** for those customers; with more time he's calm and argues for shared ownership of machines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his office-worker customers would lose their incomes three years before robots reach farm work.
Nobody would yet have worked out how to **share the gains**.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap co-op loans** so small farms can own their machines rather than rent them.
